action.description: Action object MUST contain a field `submission`, and MAY contain arbitrary additional information.

actTimeout.description: Maximum runtime (seconds) to obtain an action from an agent.

episodeSteps.description: Maximum number of steps in the episode.

includeLegalActions.description: If true, include legalActions and legalActionStrings in observations. Defaults to false since these can be derived from serializedGameAndState.

initialActions.description: Actions applied to initial state before play begins to set up starting position.

loadPresetHands.description: Repeated poker only. Load preset hand chance actions from preset_hands.jsonl.

openSpielGameName.description: The short_name of the OpenSpiel game to load.

openSpielGameParameters.description: Game parameters for Open Spiel game.

openSpielGameString.description: The full game string including parameters.

presetHands.description: Repeated poker only. List of per-hand chance action sequences to use instead of random chance.

runTimeout.description: Maximum runtime (seconds) of an episode (not necessarily DONE).

savePrompt.description: If true, the LLM prompt produced by the harness is included as a 'prompt' field on the action returned by core_harness, which causes it to be persisted in the episode replay. Defaults to false to keep replays small.

seed.description: Integer currently only used for selecting starting position.

strictMode.description: If true, agents must return only {'submission': int} (no extra fields like 'thoughts'), and per-agent TIMEOUT/ERROR/INVALID counts as a loss for the offending agent only — other agents win. If false (default), any agent error halts and voids the entire episode, matching the lenient research-mode behavior.

useImage.description: If true, indicates the observation is intended to be rendered as an image. Note that currently the agent harness is responsible for the actual rendering; no image is passed in the observation.

useOpenings.description: Whether to start from a position in an opening book.

currentPlayer.description: ID of player whose turn it is.

legalActionStrings.description: List of OpenSpiel legal action strings. Only included if includeLegalActions is true.

legalActions.description: List of OpenSpiel legal action integers. Only included if includeLegalActions is true.

openSpielGameName.description: Short name of the OpenSpiel game.

playerId.description: ID of the agent receiving this observation.

serializedGameAndState.description: Enables reconstructing the Game and State objects.

remainingOverageTime.description: Total remaining banked time (seconds) that can be used in excess of per-step actTimeouts -- agent is disqualified with TIMEOUT status when this drops below 0.

action.thoughts:
The current board is almost entirely empty, with only a single column occupied: an x at the bottom (row 5, column 3) and an o directly above it (row 4, column 3). No player has any pieces close to a win (3-in-a-row or better), and there are no threats to block. All 7 columns remain fully legal to play in.

Placing in column 3 would stack another x on top of the o (at row 3). While this re-uses the central column, it is suboptimal because the o permanently blocks any possibility of a vertical 4-in-a-row in that column. The two x's in column 3 would also be disconnected from each other vertically, limiting their future utility.

Instead, the optimal strategy in this early-game position is to maintain central control while creating flexible attacking options. Column 2 (or symmetrically column 4) is the strongest choice:
- It places an x at the bottom of column 2, immediately adjacent to the existing bottom x in column 3. This creates a 2-in-a-row horizontally along the bottom row and opens multiple diagonal lines.
- It keeps play focused on the most valuable central files (columns 2-4) without wasting a move in the already-contested column 3.
- It follows classic Connect Four opening principles after an early d1-d2 sequence, building toward later double-threats without overcommitting to a blocked line.

No deeper tactical sequence changes this evaluation at such low piece count; a full search would confirm column 2 (or 4) as among the top-evaluated moves. Column 2 is selected here for the response.

Final Answer: 2

action.thoughts:
The current board position has x pieces at the bottom of columns 2 and 3, with o pieces stacked in column 3 (rows 3 and 4). No player has a completed line of 4 yet, and it is x's turn.

Dropping an x into column 1 lands it at row 5, column 1. This creates three consecutive x pieces horizontally along the bottom row at columns 1-3. This single move generates two separate winning threats on the next turn: column 0 (completing four x's at columns 0-3) or column 4 (completing four x's at columns 1-4). Both ends are fully open.

The opponent (o) can respond in only one column per turn. If o immediately blocks one threat (e.g., column 0 or 4), x can simply take the opposite open end on the following turn to win. If o instead ignores the threats and attempts to build their own vertical line by dropping into column 3 (creating three o's at rows 2-4 in column 3), x blocks that threat by dropping into column 3 at row 1. o is then forced to block one of x's horizontal threats on their next turn, after which x takes the remaining open end to complete four in a row and win.

No other single move creates an equivalent forcing position (two threats) this quickly, and o has no immediate winning response or fork of their own. Column 1 is therefore optimal.

Final Answer: 1
